title: India's Economy on Track for 7% Growth in FY27 Despite Global Headwinds, EY Says
excerpt: A recent EY report projects India's real GDP growth at 7-7.2% in FY27, supported by robust industrial output, a government capex rebound, and strong credit growth, even as inflation and weaker trade conditions pose risks.
body:
• EY projects India's real GDP growth at 7-7.2% for FY27, with nominal GDP growth at 12.5-13%.
  • Industrial production expanded 7.3% in June 2026, the fastest pace in 23 months, with manufacturing output up 7.8%.
  • Government capital expenditure rebounded sharply, growing 23.7% in Q1 FY27 after contracting 23.3% in the prior quarter.
  • Wholesale price inflation at 9.8% and a potentially widening current account deficit remain key risks to monitor.

India's economy is expected to grow at 7-7.2% in real terms during FY27, according to a recent report by EY, with robust industrial activity and a sharp rebound in government capital spending underpinning a growth outlook that remains strong relative to global peers.

The consulting firm pegged nominal GDP growth at 12.5-13%, noting that India's prospects hold up even as geopolitical uncertainty, elevated crude oil prices, and a weaker global trade environment pose headwinds.

Industrial Output Hits 23-Month High

A stronger performance by the industrial sector has bolstered the growth picture. India's Index of Industrial Production expanded 7.3% in June 2026, its fastest pace in 23 months. Industrial growth averaged 5.7% during the first quarter of FY27, its strongest showing in eight quarters.

"India's Index of Industrial Production expanded 7.3% in June 2026, its fastest pace in 23 months."

Manufacturing was a key driver, with output rising 7.8%. Electrical equipment, motor vehicles, textiles, and food products were among the better-performing segments.

There are signs, however, that the pace of expansion may be moderating. The manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index fell to 53.5 in July from 54.2 in June, while the services PMI dropped to 53.3 from 57.4. Both readings remained above the 50-point threshold separating expansion from contraction, but the direction of movement bears watching.

Government Capex Rebounds

Government spending has provided another key pillar of support. Capital expenditure growth surged to 23.7% in the first quarter of FY27, reversing a 23.3% contraction in the fourth quarter of FY26. The fiscal deficit stood at 18.2% of the annual budget target during the quarter.

The renewed push on capital expenditure should help sustain demand and strengthen the outlook for real GDP growth, EY said. Credit conditions also remained supportive, with gross bank credit growth accelerating to 18.6% in June — its highest level in 25 months.

Inflation and External Risks

Inflation remains a key risk to the outlook. Consumer price inflation stood at 4.4% in July, while wholesale price inflation reached 9.8%, driven by mineral oils, food articles, metals, chemicals, and fuels.

The elevated WPI reading could push nominal GDP growth above the government's budget assumption of 10.04%, EY said. That would support revenue receipts and could enable the government to continue its capital expenditure program while maintaining fiscal deficit targets.

The external sector presents a more mixed picture. Higher energy costs and weaker global demand may weigh on exports, while India's current account deficit could widen to 1.9% of GDP in FY27, based on OECD projections.

Import Substitution Opportunity

EY outlined a long-term path to improving India's external position, identifying 1,272 products where targeted efforts could potentially replace about $189 billion worth of imports. Greater export promotion and expanded domestic manufacturing could help reduce supply-side vulnerabilities over the medium term, the firm said.

The combination of fiscal discipline and sustained capital spending has been a differentiator for India among emerging economies, and the latest data reinforces that trajectory at a time when several large economies face ballooning deficits and slowing growth.
